gbs333-a82229-d1e107.summary: This is the formal enunciation of the question, restating in the running text the same question already given in the heading: whether being everywhere and in all things through essence, presence, and power belongs to God alone.

gbs333-a82229-d1e120.summary: Opens with the customary division of the question into three articles, then states as certain among theologians that it is proper to God alone to be in all existing and possible things through essence, presence, and power. It flags one special difficulty reserved for later treatment: whether God's being in all things through power, as their immediate cause, entails that he is also everywhere through essence.
claims: The question, as is customary, divides into three articles.
It is certain among theologians that being in all existing and possible things through essence, presence, and power is proper to God alone.
A special difficulty remains: whether God's being in all things through power (as their immediate cause) entails that he is everywhere through essence.

gbs333-a82229-d1e145.summary: Reports Lombard's threefold division, drawn from the authorities of the saints, of God's existence in creatures: a general mode by which God conserves all creatures, a special mode of assistance by which God indwells holy souls (through grace), and a singular mode of union by which, in assuming human nature, God joins it to himself in unity of person (Christ). It locates each mode textually: the singular mode belongs to book III, the special mode was already treated at distinction 19, and the present question concerns the general mode.
claims: Lombard distinguishes a threefold existence of God in creatures: general, special, and singular.
By general existence God conserves all creatures.
By special existence (assistance) God indwells holy souls.
By singular existence God, assuming human nature, unites it to himself in unity of person in Christ.
The singular mode is deferred to book III; the special mode was treated at distinction 19; the present question treats the general mode.

gbs333-a82229-d1e171.summary: Sets out a threefold sense in which one thing can be said to be 'in' another: by power, by presence, or by essence. Being-in-by-power means being subject to another's power, which can hold even across local distance (the sun's power over lower bodies, a king's power over his realm), though this usage is not common among philosophers. Being-in-by-presence has two senses: presence of cognition (a thing is sufficiently present to know or be known, as an object is 'in' a cognitive power when actually known though really distant) and presence of local non-distance (place and the thing located are mutually 'in' one another), the latter being the more usual philosophical usage, chiefly for the located-in-place direction. A closing analogy notes that some general terms are, by common usage, applied more readily to some of their referents than to others (e.g. 'animal' more to brutes than to humans in popular speech), foreshadowing an analogous asymmetry in how 'esse in' terms will be applied.
claims: Something can be in another in three ways: by power, by presence, or by essence.
Being-in-by-power means being subject to another's power, even at local distance (e.g., the sun over things below, a king over his kingdom), though this usage is uncommon among philosophers.
Being-in-by-presence-of-cognition means being sufficiently present to know or to be known by another.
Being-in-by-presence-of-non-distance means the mutual local indistance of place and located thing, the more usual philosophical usage (more so for the located-in-place direction than the reverse).
General terms are sometimes, by common usage, applied more readily to some things falling under them than to others.
concepts: modes of esse in alio: potentia, praesentia, essentia

gbs333-a82229-d1e254.summary: Defines esse per essentiam: to be in something (not caused by it) without being distant from it by anything intrinsic to oneself, such that wherever the thing is, the one 'in' it (or something belonging to it) is also there. Form is said to be in matter per essentiam in exactly this sense: wherever matter, or any part of matter, exists, form exists there too. This differs from the relation of a located thing to its place, since a located thing is, in some respect, distant from part of its place, and conversely.
claims: To be in something per essentiam means to be in it (not caused by it) and not distant from it by anything intrinsic, such that wherever the thing is, the one in it (or something of it) is there.
Form is said to be in matter per essentiam because wherever matter, or a part of matter, is, there form is.
This is distinct from the relation of a located thing to place, since the located thing is, in some respect, distant from part of the place, and conversely.

gbs333-a82229-d1e278.summary: Notes an equivocation in 'per essentiam' not intended in this question: it can mean 'per se' (a necessary, essential predication, as man is per essentiam an animal and rational), or it can mean 'immediately' (as the soul is said per essentiam to be capable of discipline, because its essence is that to which being disciplinable immediately belongs). Neither sense is meant here; only the essential, non-distant presence explained in the preceding paragraph is at issue.
claims: 'Per essentiam' can equivocally mean 'per se' (necessary, essential predication).
'Per essentiam' can also mean 'immediately' (as the soul is per essentiam capable of discipline).
Neither of these senses is intended in the present question; only the sense of essential, non-distant presence explained earlier applies.

gbs333-a82229-d1e302.summary: Lays out, following the Lombard's text, three ways something can be in a place: commensurative/circumscriptive (its parts correspond to the parts of place, as with a body quantitatively in place); terminative/definitive (it is really where the place is and not naturally apt to be simultaneously elsewhere; angelic spirits and rational souls are in place in this superior mode); and repletive (it is really present in a place by substance without being confined to it, being simultaneously in every other place, even by its own nature). It notes that the qualifier 'naturally apt' in the second mode is needed because God's power can exceptionally multiply a body in several places at once (as Christ's body in the sacrament) without this reflecting a natural aptitude, since supernatural power confers no natural aptitude. What is in place by either of the first two modes is called 'local' and mutable with respect to place; what is in place by the third mode is not.
claims: Something can be in place in three ways: commensuratively/circumscriptively, terminatively/definitively, or repletively.
Commensurative presence: the thing's parts correspond to the parts of place, as with bodies.

Terminative/definitive presence: the thing is really where the place is and not naturally apt to be elsewhere at once; angelic spirits and rational souls are in place this way, a mode superior to the first.

The qualifier 'naturally apt' is needed because divine power can exceptionally multiply a body in several places (e.g., Christ's body in the sacrament) without this reflecting natural aptitude, since supernatural power confers no natural aptitude.
Repletive presence: the thing is really present in a place by substance without confinement to it, being simultaneously in every other place even by its own nature.
What is in place by the first two modes is called local and mutable with respect to place; what is in place by the third mode is not.
concepts: modes of esse in loco: circumscriptive, definitive, repletive

gbs333-a82229-d1e373.summary: Opens article 2 with its first conclusion: God is in all things through power. The proof is a simple syllogism: God is the cause of all things, and to be in another through power just is to be able to produce, conserve, or act upon it (as established in the earlier notandum on potentia); therefore God is potentially in all things.
claims: Article 2, first conclusion: God is in all things through power.
Proof: God is the cause of all things; being-in-another-through-power consists precisely in the ability to produce, conserve, or act upon that other; therefore God is in all things through power.

gbs333-a82229-d1e393.summary: Second conclusion of article 2: God is in all things through presence, in both senses distinguished earlier (cognitive presence and presence of non-distance). Cognitive presence follows because God knows all things distinctly. Presence of non-distance is argued, on Augustine's authority, by exhaustive division: God is present to no thing in that mode, or to some but not others, or to all. The first is excluded because no existing thing can be posited that is nowhere and distant from everything else. The second is excluded because, were God present to one thing and not another, he would have to be either finite with respect to it (impossible, since he is unlimited and infinite) or not finite yet newly present to something previously absent from — which would entail local motion in God, an impossibility. Hence God is present to all things.
claims: Article 2, second conclusion: God is in all things through presence, in both the cognitive and non-distance senses explained earlier.
God's cognitive presence follows from his distinctly knowing all things.

By an argument attributed to Augustine, God's presence-of-non-distance to all things is established by excluding the alternatives that he is present to nothing or to some but not others, since either alternative leads to absurdity (an existent distant from everything, or a change of local presence in an infinite, unlimited being).

gbs333-a82229-d1e435.summary: Third conclusion of article 2: God is everywhere and in all things through his essence. This follows from the previous conclusion (that God is present to all such that distant from none), and is confirmed by Jeremiah 23:24, 'I fill heaven and earth.' The conclusion is also held as an article of faith, as the magister (Lombard) shows by many authorities.
claims: Article 2, third conclusion: God is everywhere and in all things through his essence.
This follows from God's being present to all things such that distant from none, and is confirmed by Jeremiah 23:24.
The conclusion is also an article of faith, per Lombard's citation of many authorities.

gbs333-a82229-d1e453.summary: Fourth conclusion of article 2: God is in every place repletively, not locally, definitively, commensuratively, or mobilely. Proof: God can be absent from no place and cannot be terminated or circumscribed by any place; consequently his presence in place is repletive rather than local, and he is immobile with respect to place, since he can neither be moved to nor from any place nor be absent from any.
claims: Article 2, fourth conclusion: God is in every place repletively, not locally, definitively, commensuratively, or mobilely.
Proof: God can be absent from no place and cannot be terminated or circumscribed by any place, hence his presence is repletive and immobile with respect to place.

gbs333-a82229-d1e479.summary: Opens article 3. Although it is certain by faith among theologians that God is everywhere (cited from Ps. 138:7, 'Where shall I go from your spirit?'), two difficulties remain. The first: does God's being in all things through power, i.e. as their immediate cause, entail that he is everywhere through essence? Some, following what is attributed to Aquinas (ST I, q.8, a.3), say yes, on the principle that mover and moved must be together (Aristotle, Phys. VII), since God is present to all as cause of being. The author rejects this as not universally true, since not every mover must be together with what it moves, whether among corporeal agents or agents acting through intellect and will. Ockham and Scotus are cited as proving that the sun immediately causes light in things below without requiring the co-presence the argument assumes. Regarding intellectual agency: if willing alone sufficed to produce an effect, one could remain in one place (Tübingen) and will, and thereby produce, an effect in a distant place (Stuttgart); hence, even if God were not present per essentiam to an effect but confined to one determinate place in heaven, he could still produce and conserve everything below just as he actually does.
claims: Article 3 treats two remaining difficulties beyond the faith-certain conclusion (Ps. 138:7) that God is everywhere.
First difficulty: does God's being in all things by power (as immediate cause) entail that he is everywhere by essence?
Aquinas (ST I, q.8, a.3) is cited as answering yes, on the Aristotelian principle (Phys. VII) that mover and moved must be together.
The author denies the inference is universally valid, since not every mover need be together with what it moves, in corporeal or intellectual/volitional agency alike.
Ockham and Scotus are cited to show the sun immediately causes light in things below without the co-presence the principle would require.

By analogy with willing-at-a-distance (e.g., willing in Tübingen an effect in Stuttgart), God could produce and conserve all things below even if confined per essentiam to one place, just as he actually does now.
concepts: action at a distance by intellect and will

gbs333-a82229-d1e549.summary: Responds to the Aristotelian objection (Phys. VII) by restricting its scope: Aristotle speaks only of physical agents, which act through active and passive qualities and through contact producing an effect of the same kind (univocal) in both the terminus and the medium. Fuller treatment is deferred to book II.
claims: The Aristotelian mover-moved co-presence principle (Phys. VII) applies only to physical agents acting through active/passive qualities via contact, producing a univocal effect in terminus and medium.
Fuller treatment of this point is deferred to book II.

gbs333-a82229-d1e566.summary: States the doctor's (Ockham's) resulting conclusion: it is not the case that God is in all things through essence precisely and solely because he is their cause, as if the inference were a formal consequence, 'this acts on this, therefore this is in this, or is present to this.'
claims: The doctor (Ockham) concludes that God's essential presence in all things does not follow, by formal consequence, from his causing all things; 'X acts on Y' does not formally imply 'X is in Y' or 'X is present to Y.'

gbs333-a82229-d1e579.summary: Introduces the second difficulty of article 3: whether being in all created things (other than itself) through power, presence, and essence is proper to God. Two senses of 'belonging' are distinguished: simply/contingently, i.e. that, under some case or through some power, the subject is in all things; or necessarily, i.e. that being-in-all-existing-things follows necessarily from the subject's own being, such that it cannot exist without being in all existing things, nor can anything exist in which it is not.
claims: Second difficulty: is being-in-all-things through power, presence, and essence proper to God alone?

Two senses of belonging are distinguished: (1) simply/contingently — under some case or power, something is in all things; (2) necessarily — being-in-all-existing-things follows necessarily from the subject's own being.

gbs333-a82229-d1e614.summary: Gives the first conclusion on the second difficulty: being in all created things through power, presence, and essence in the first (contingent) sense is not proper to God. Proof: this mode is communicable to a creature by divine power, since it implies no contradiction that some created intelligence concur in producing and conserving all creatures to which it co-assists, and that only such creatures exist — in which case that intelligence would itself be in all existing created things through power, etc.
claims: Conclusion 1 (second difficulty): being-in-all-things in the first, contingent sense is not proper to God alone.

Proof: divine power could communicate this mode to a creature, since it is not contradictory that a created intelligence concur in producing and conserving all creatures (co-assisting to them) if only such creatures existed, in which case that intelligence would be in all of them through power.

gbs333-a82229-d1e643.summary: Adds a further supporting argument for the preceding conclusion: God could replicate a body in diverse places, and just as to several places, so to all — a point argued at length elsewhere (lecture 46, in the exposition of the canon of the Mass).
claims: Further support: God could replicate a body to diverse places, and by extension to all places, as argued at length in lecture 46 on the exposition of the canon of the Mass.

gbs333-a82229-d1e652.summary: Gives a further supporting argument: if nothing existed in the world except a single man, his soul would then be 'everywhere' in that world, i.e. throughout his body, since all the body's parts are subject to it and it is intimately present to the body — illustrating that the contingent sense of universal presence could belong to a creature under a limiting supposition.
claims: Further argument: if nothing existed besides a single man, his soul would be present throughout the whole body, since all the body's parts are subject to the soul and it is intimately present to the body.
This confirms that contingent universal presence (in the first sense) is not unique to God, since it could be satisfied by a created soul under a limiting supposition.

gbs333-a82229-d1e665.summary: Gives the second conclusion on the second difficulty: being in all created things through power, essence, and presence in the second (necessary) sense is proper to God alone, since no creature is necessarily in all things besides itself; Ambrose and other saints, in attributing universal presence to God alone, speak in this necessary sense, which also preserves Aquinas's dictum (ST I, q.8, a.4) that being everywhere, first and per se, is proper to God alone. An objection is then raised against this conclusion: what belongs to something per essentiam belongs to it necessarily and always, yet God's being-in-all-things does not hold always, since not before the world's constitution.
claims: Conclusion 2 (second difficulty): being-in-all-things in the second, necessary sense is proper to God alone.

Proof: no creature is necessarily in all things besides itself; Ambrose and other saints, in ascribing universal presence to God alone, speak in this necessary sense — which also preserves Aquinas's dictum (ST I, q.8, a.4).

Objection: what belongs to something per essentiam belongs to it necessarily and always, yet God's being-in-all-things does not hold before the world's constitution, seemingly contradicting the conclusion.
concepts: objection from the temporality of creation

gbs333-a82229-d1e705.summary: Raises two further objections against the second conclusion. First, an argument by analogy: as an informable-by-quality thing relates to what has the quality, so being-in-place relates to what has place; but what is informed by a quality is necessarily alterable according to it, so what is in place must be necessarily mobile according to place — yet God is not mobile according to place, seemingly undermining the conclusion. Second, it is argued that universal presence cannot be proper to God because it belongs also to the universal, which is everywhere through essence and, consequently, through power in whatever way it has power.
claims: Objection A: by analogy with quality-in-subject (which entails alterability), being-in-place should entail mobility according to place; but God is immobile according to place, apparently conflicting with his being essentially in place.
Objection B: universal presence cannot be proper to God alone, since the universal itself is everywhere through essence and, consequently, through power.

gbs333-a82229-d1e744.summary: Replies to the objection from temporality: God's essential universal presence does not mean he is in all things necessarily and always, including before creation (when he was in no creature, since none existed); rather it means only that it is repugnant for God to exist without being in whatever does exist — the conditional necessity already explained, not an absolute, atemporal one.
claims: Reply to the temporality objection: God's essential presence does not entail being in all things necessarily and always (including before the world's constitution); it means only that it is repugnant for God to exist without being in whatever exists — a conditional, not absolute, necessity.
concepts: presence conditioned on the existence of creatures

gbs333-a82229-d1e762.summary: Replies to the mobility objection: God is in place immutably, and the analogy drawn from quality does not hold, because having a quality involves receiving in oneself an inhering accidental form distinct from oneself, whose reception or loss constitutes alteration; but being in place involves receiving nothing intrinsic. Hence something can be in place without thereby being mobile according to place, so long as the place itself remains (as in God's case) — unlike a quality, which, since God can separate any two really distinct things, can always in principle be lost.
claims: Reply to the mobility objection: the quality-subject analogy fails because having a quality involves receiving an inhering, distinct accidental form (whose reception/loss is alteration), while being in place involves receiving nothing intrinsic.

Something can therefore be in place without being mobile with respect to place, provided the place itself remains — unlike a quality, always losable in principle since God can separate really distinct things.
concepts: divine power to separate distinct things

gbs333-a82229-d1e791.summary: Replies to the objection from universals: the universal itself is not everywhere, nor does Aristotle intend this; rather what is common, as universal, is said to be 'everywhere' only in the sense that it is predicated of any singular contained under it, wherever that singular exists (wherever the singular 'man' exists, 'humanity' is predicated there) — it is not thereby required that the common nature 'man' itself literally exist everywhere.
claims: Reply to the universal objection: the universal itself is not everywhere; Aristotle does not intend this.
The universal is said to be 'everywhere' only in the sense that it is predicated of any singular instance, wherever that singular exists — not that the universal itself as such exists in every place.

gbs333-a82229.summary: Quaestio 1 asks whether being everywhere and in all things through essence, presence, and power is proper to God alone. Three preliminary notanda set the terms: the question divides into three articles; the magister's threefold (general/special/singular) existence of God in creatures situates the present inquiry as concerning the general mode; and being-in-another is distinguished into modes by power, presence (cognitive and of non-distance), and essence, together with three modes of being in place (circumscriptive, definitive, repletive). Article 2 establishes, by four conclusions, that God is in all things through power (as their cause), through presence (cognitively and by non-distance, per an Augustinian argument excluding partial presence), through essence (confirmed by Jer. 23:24 and held de fide), and in every place repletively rather than locally or mobilely. Article 3 takes up two difficulties. The first asks whether God's immediate causal power over all things entails his essential omnipresence; against the inference attributed to Aquinas (from the principle that mover and moved must be together), the author, following Ockham and Scotus, denies the entailment, restricting the Aristotelian principle to physical agents and showing by the analogy of willing-at-a-distance that causal immediacy does not require essential presence. The second difficulty asks whether universal presence is proper to God, distinguishing a contingent sense (communicable to a creature, as illustrated by a hypothetical sole co-causing intelligence, divine multilocation of a body, and a soul in a world containing only one man) from a necessary sense (proper to God alone, per Ambrose and Aquinas). Three objections to this second conclusion — from the temporality of creation, from an analogy with quality that would make God locally mobile, and from the ubiquity of universals — are each answered: God's necessity here is conditional, not absolute; the quality analogy fails because place involves no intrinsic reception; and the universal's 'ubiquity' is merely predicative, not the universal's own real presence everywhere.
claims: It is certain among theologians, and an article of faith, that being in all existing and possible things necessarily and essentially through power, presence, and essence is proper to God alone; that God is present to all such things repletively and immovably.

God's immediate causal power over all things does not, by formal logical consequence, entail his essential omnipresence — against the inference attributed to Aquinas and in agreement with Ockham and Scotus.

Being-in-all-things belongs properly and necessarily to God alone only in the sense that it is repugnant for God to exist without being in whatever exists (a conditional necessity), not in a sense entailing that he is in all things absolutely and always, nor in a sense incommunicable in principle to a creature under the weaker, contingent reading of universal presence.
concepts: Ockham and Scotus vs. the Thomist inference
necessity vs. contingency of universal presence
